newsitem.title: USA: Turkish economy seen fragile, major reforms needed.
newsitem.headline: Turkish economy seen fragile, major reforms needed.

text.p: Turkey, facing high inflation and big social security deficits, needs far-reaching economic reforms to realise its potential, a Washington-based international monetary source said on Thursday.

The source, speaking a day after the International Monetary Fund reviewed the Turkish economy, told Reuters a more open economy and "suitcase trade" -- trade in goods bought in Turkey by individual visitors from the former Soviet Union -- were providing some economic relief.

But the government still faced major problems. "The message is that Turkey needs to adopt a comprehensive programme of reforms in order to realise its potential -- that was the message last year and it remains so this year," the source, who declined to be further identified, told Reuters.

"They face a fairly fragile overall economic situation. High inflation, leading to increasing income disparities, is preventing the country from realising its potential, which everybody considers to be good. The message is that they must urgently tackle these problems."

The source said the government needed to reform the deficit-hit social security system, push ahead with privatisation and strengthen state banks, including by introducing changes to agricultural subsidy programmes.

Banking sources in Istanbul this week highlighted similar issues as problems and said they would be addressed in the IMF review. The IMF does not as a rule release its annual reviews of a country's economy, although some details are sometimes made available about 10 days after the IMF board meets to discuss a specific country.

The new Turkish government has already revised its economic targets for 1997 and the Washington source said the new figures were "more realistic" than the previous ones. The government is targeting end-year 1997 inflation of 80-85 percent, up from a previous forecast of 57.7 percent.
Finance Minister Zekeriya Temizel on Wednesday forecast a 1997 budget deficit of 2,400 trillion lira ($15.9 billion), almost twice the 1996 shortfall of 1,218 trillion lira.
"The new forecasts are just taking account of reality," the Washington source said. "It's more or less what most observers ... are looking for."

He said initial targets had been based on overly optimistic revenue projections and optimistic assumptions on privatisation. It was too early to give forecasts for 1998, as much would depend on the policies of the new government.

The source said positive elements included a dynamic private sector and strong economic growth. Turkey's external position was probably "better than people generally had thought" because of the suitcase traders, who travel across the borders with bags and cases stuffed with consumer goods.

"The economy has some elements of strength. Over the years it has become more open ... but it is plagued by chronic high inflation and has quite a number of weaknesses," he said. "It's not an entirely bleak picture but it is not a reassuring picture either."
